title: Few-shot Unlearning
abstract: We consider the problem of machine unlearning to erase the impact of a target dataset, used in training but incorrect or sensitive, from a trained model. It has been often presumed that every data sample to erase or remain is entirely identifiable and thus clarifies the desired model behavior after unlearning. However, such a flawless identification can be infeasible in practice. We pose a further realistic yet challenging scenario, referred to as few-shot unlearning, where only a few samples of target data are provided while aiming at achieving the underlying intention (e.g., correcting mislabels, countering a certain privacy attack, or specifying nothing) behind the full target dataset. We then devise a few-shot unlearning method including a new model inversion technique, specialized for unlearning scenarios, to retrieve a proxy of the training dataset from the trained model if needed. We demonstrate that our method using only a tiny subset of target data can achieve similar performance to the state-of-the-art methods with full access to target data. Our code and results are available at https://github.com/ml-postech/Few-shot-Unlearning. 3276 2024 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

We consider the problem of machine unlearning to erase the impact of a target dataset, used in training but incorrect or sensitive, from a trained model. It has been often presumed that every data sample to erase or remain is entirely identifiable and thus clarifies the desired model behavior after unlearning. However, such a flawless identification can be in- feasible in practice. We pose a further realistic yet challenging scenario, referred to as few-shot unlearning , where only a few samples of target data are provided while aiming at achieving the underlying intention ( e.g., correcting mislabels, countering a certain privacy attack, or specifying nothing) behind the full target dataset. We then devise a few-shot unlearning method including a new model inversion technique, specialized for unlearning scenarios, to retrieve a proxy of the training dataset from the trained model if needed. We demonstrate that our method using only a tiny subset of target data can achieve similar performance to the state-of-the-art methods with full access to target data. Our code and results are available at https://github.com/ml-postech/Few-shot-Unlearning. 1. Introduction Machine unlearning is the task of excising a specific target dataset from a trained model. The goal is to mitigate unwanted behaviors of the model that may have been in- duced by the target samples, which are, e.g., mislabeled [1], [2] or privacy-sensitive (c.f., right to be forgotten [3]). While retraining a model from scratch without using the target data is a straightforward solution, it is often impossible to do so whenever the original training data is not fully accessible due to memory cost or privacy concerns. To this end, standard unlearning algorithms aim to approximate such oracle retrained model by utilizing limited [4], [5], [6] or no [7] access to training data. Prior works have demon- strated that such unlearning can be successfully performed, whenever a complete indication of the target data is given to clearly specify the response to target or remaining data after unlearning. However, such a clear indication of the unlearning target is often restricted. For example, when a model has been ∗ equal contribution Figure 1: Confusing 7 's (left) and 2's (right) in MNIST dataset [8]. trained on multiple randomly augmented versions ( e.g., via random cropping) of each sample, retrieving all the aug- mented versions of the target data used for training may not be possible unless the augmentation history has been stored during the training. As another example, one can consider online learning scenarios being fed a stream of data that is not stored due to a shortage of storage space or privacy concerns. Besides these recording limitations, the target data can be overwhelmingly many to be minutely specified in the training dataset. With the limited access to target samples, i.e., few- shot unlearning, the desired model behavior on inaccessible samples is prone to be ill-specified. For instance, consider a classifier trained with a spoiled MNIST dataset of handwrit- ten digits (0-9) where hundreds of crossed-seven, denoted by 7 , are mislabeled as 2, c.f., Figure 1. Given a target dataset consisting of only few images of 7 with label 2, the response to 7 after the standard unlearning may still be 2, as the remaining dataset after excluding only the few target data still includes hundreds of the mislabeled 7 . Meanwhile, the unlearning requester might have different intentions beyond unlearning the few target data, such as (i) a standard unlearning to exclude the influence of all the mislabeled 7; (ii) a mislabel correction to let 7 be classified as 7; or (iii) a countering against a privacy attack on 7 . Standard unlearning frameworks lack an explicit mechanism to account for these underlying intentions of the unlearner. In addition, even when all the samples of 7 are identified and requested to be erased, the response of the retrained model to the erased samples can be still ill-determined and possibly changing over training epochs (see Section 6.1). To address these challenges, we first establish a gener- alized formulation of the few-shot unlearning that can take into account the intention of unlearning (Section 3), and 3276 DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00182 encompass not only the standard unlearning with a complete target indication as a special case but also unlearning with specific intentions to correct mislabels or to defend against privacy attacks. Based on this formulation, we propose a framework (Section 4) consisting of (i) model inversion to retrieve a proxy for training data from all the information available in the context of unlearning including the given model and target samples (Section 4.1); (ii) filtration to divide the retrieved proxy data into a part to be preserved and the other to be unlearned or modified according to unlearner's intention while augmenting the few target sam- ples (Section 4.2); and then (iii) relearning with the filtered proxy data to scrub out the unwanted behavior and impose the intended one onto the augmented target dataset (Sec- tion 4.3). For the model inversion step, we design a new inversion technique specialized for unlearning, that fully utilizes the knowledge at hand in the context of unlearning: the trained model, the target samples, and the general prior on the data domain. In the relearning step, we devise a set of relearning strategies, which relabels the augmented target dataset differently from the filtration step, to impose unlearner's intention accordingly: Ours std for the standard unlearning; Ours def and Ours unt for explicit protection from a privacy attack, namely, membership inference attack [9]; Oursneg and Ours cor for mislabel correction. In our experiments of standard and few-shot unlearning setups with canonical deep learning models (Section 5), we validate the superiority of our method compared to existing ones [4], [10], [11] with almost full access to the training and target datasets. We also demonstrate a sharp unlearning to erase only subclass such as 7 , which is infeasible in previous methods [12], [13] with no access to the training dataset. In particular, only our method can successfully unlearn a subset ( e.g., 7 's) of class. Our empirical study suggests appropriate designs of unlearning methods for each of the useful intentions: standard unlearning, mislabel cor- rection, and privacy attack protection. This provides a uni- fied view of existing works implicitly postulating different intentions, e.g., standard unlearning [11], [14] and privacy attack protection [10]. In addition, the formulation with the notion of intention allows us to newly discover practical unlearning methods to correct the mislabeled target dataset (Oursneg), applicable at no extra cost of annotations, and to protect the target data from the privacy attack (Ours def), while preserving the accuracy. Contributions. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: • We establish the few-shot unlearning problem that embraces not only the standard unlearning but also the various explicit intentions such as privacy attack protection and mislabel correction. • We devise the unlearning framework, consisting of the model inversion, filtration, and relearning steps, each of which is tailored to address the few-shot unlearning problem with useful intention: Ours neg for mislabel correction and Ours def for privacy attack protection. • In our experiment, we show the strength of our method in both few-shot and standard unlearning setups with various intentions even compared to existing methods with full access to the training datasets. We also cor- roborate that given only a trained model and few target samples, our method enables a sophisticated unlearning to eliminate a subclass, that is previously intractable. 2. Related Work Machine unlearning. In the landscape of machine unlearn- ing, the research trajectory has evolved with different levels of assumptions on data availability. Assuming that the full training dataset D and the target dataset De ⊂ D are fully accessible [6], [10], [11], [14], [15], [16], unlearning problems have been posed to reduce the computational cost of unlearning, compared to that of retraining from scratch with the remaining dataset Dr := D \ De. Meanwhile, such full access to D is often restricted due to privacy concerns or limited memory. Hence, there have been extensive efforts to alleviate this strong assumption by replacing the full access to D with certain proxies of D [4], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], sample-wise training history [22], [23] or Bayesian assumptions [5], [7]. Recently, [13] addressed a zero-shot unlearning to erase all samples of a specific class without seeing any training sample in D nor De, which was possible as the target and remaining dataset are fully characterized by labels, i.e., a fine-grained unlearning to erase only a subclass ( e.g., 7 ) is not possible. To our best knowledge, our method is the first to address the few-shot unlearning problem, including such a fine-grained unlearning, given few target samples and no additional information on D other than the original model trained on D. Model inversion. With growing scales of machine learning datasets and increasing attention to privacy concerns, model inversion has been widely studied under various contexts. The model inversion is particularly useful for applications that require a data-free transfer learning, including model compression [24], [25], [26], [27], [28], [29], [30] and continual learning [27]. The problem of privacy leakage detection can also be formulated as inverting data from the model [31], [32] or even gradients [33]. In this line of works on model inversion, an extensive set of prior and side information on data domain ( e.g., implicit [34] and explicit [35] image domain priors and batch norm statistics [27]) have been exploited to improve inverted data quality via reducing the search space. Building upon these advances, recent studies [36], [37] have demonstrated the effectiveness of leveraging public data in enhancing the performance of model inversion. We draw inspirations from this methodol- ogy to devise a new model inversion technique specialized for the unlearning scenario, where we use target samples as an additional hint on the training dataset. The developed technique may be of independent interest to other data- free model inversion algorithms if few samples of training dataset are allowed, while it is also possible to enhance our model inversion for unlearning based on the recent advances in model inversion [36], [37]. 3277
